full_text: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men. MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records.EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality.Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.”Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Study designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Supplementary MaterialSupplementary information are available at https://www.scielo.br/10.48331/SCIELODATA.EOBWJF Supplementary PDF RESULTSIn 2023, 2,792 adult cancer patients underwent anti-HBs serological testing at ICESP. Of these, 327 were excluded because anti-HBc testing had not been performed, 253 because they were anti-HBc-reactive, and 33 because they were HBsAg-reactive. Although 2,179 patients met the initial serological criteria, 1,036 were excluded because they resided outside Sao Paulo city. Consequently, the final study population comprised 1,143 patients who met all inclusion and exclusion criteria.Among included patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, and 60.6% self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 76.8% of cases, whereas hematological malignancies accounted for 19.4%. Patients were distributed across all zones of the city, with the largest proportions residing in the South (29.7%) and East (25.0%) (Supplementary Table S1).Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the highest proportions were observed in the South (28.9%, 98/339) and East (28.7%, 82/286), whereas the lowest was observed in the North (20.7%, 51/246). The regional distribution and corresponding 95% CI are presented in Figure 1.In the univariable Poisson regression, serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B was less frequently observed among patients residing in the North than those residing in the South (20.7% versus 28.9%; PR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51-1.01, p = 0.054).However, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders in the multivariable Poisson model (p = 0.139), indicating no independent association between zone of residence and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. In contrast, age group and sex remained independently associated with the outcome (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Compared with patients aged ≥ 60 years, those aged 18-39 years were more likely to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (adjusted PR [aPR] = 3.56, 95% CI: 2.66-4.77), whereas patients aged 40-59 years were also more likely to present the outcome (aPR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.30-2.31). Likewise, female patients were more likely than male patients to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (aPR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10-1.82).No statistically significant differences were observed in the distribution of age (p = 0.184), sex (p = 0.504), ethnicity/skin color (p = 0.835), or primary cancer type (p = 0.340) across the five zones of Sao Paulo city (Table 2). Descriptively, the West had the highest proportion of younger adults (18-39 years, 20.5%), whereas the North had the highest proportion of older adults (≥ 60 years, 55.3%). Female patients, White patients, and patients with solid tumors predominated across all regions. Likewise, despite slight descriptive variation in the proportion of patients with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B across the five zones (Figure 1), no statistically significant regional differences were observed (p = 0.180). full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTVaccination is the primary strategy for preventing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, but its frequency remains insufficiently characterized among cancer patients. This study evaluated the regional distribution of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city, Brazil. We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) serological testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity was defined as reactive anti-HBs and non-reactive hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc). Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were performed to identify associated factors. Among 1,143 patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, 60.6% self-identified White, and 76.8% had solid tumors. Overall, 26.2% of cancer patients had serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the North Zone had a lower frequency than the South Zone (20.7% versus 28.9%), although regional differences were not statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. Female sex (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.23-2.27, p = 0.001) and younger age (18-39 years versus ≥ 60 years: aPR = 6.89, 95% CI: 4.72-10.95, p < 0.001) were independently associated with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings indicate a low frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients across Sao Paulo, particularly among older adults and men.
full_text_sections.methods: MATERIALS AND METHODSStudy designThis retrospective observational study included adult cancer patients receiving care at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP), affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the Faculty of Medicine, University of Sao Paulo (HCFMUSP), between January and December 2023. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records.EthicsThis study was approved by the Ethics Committee for Analysis of Research Projects of the HCFMUSP under protocols No 6.120.828 and 6.718.762 (CAAE: 70101521.9.0000.0068). Requirement for informed consent was waived, and all data were de-identified before analysis to ensure patient confidentiality.Data sourcePatients with solid tumors or hematologic malignancies who attended the ICESP, aged 18 years or older and who underwent anti-HBs serological testing were eligible for inclusion. Patients without anti-HBc testing or with reactive anti-HBc or hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) results were excluded, as were those who did not reside in Sao Paulo city. All eligible patients who met the inclusion and exclusion criteria during the study period (January to December 2023) were consecutively identified and included; therefore, no sampling strategy was applied.Demographic characteristics (i.e., age, sex [sex assigned at birth], and ethnicity/skin color), primary cancer type (i.e., solid tumors or hematological malignancies), and residential zone within Sao Paulo city were retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. Ethnicity/skin color was classified according to participants’ self-identification using the Brazilian census classification system: Brazilians of African origin who self-identified as “Black,” Indigenous Brazilians who self-identified as “Indigenous,” Brazilians of mixed ethnic background who self-identified as “Pardo” (“Brown/Mixed-ethnicity”), Brazilians of European origin who self-identified as “White,” and Brazilians of Asian origin who self-identified as “Asian.”Statistical analysisAge was analyzed both as a continuous variable and as a categorical variable (18-39, 40-59, and ≥ 60 years). Sex was classified as male or female; ethnicity/skin color as White or non-White (including Black, Indigenous, Pardo, and Asian); and primary cancer type as hematological malignancies or solid tumors.Associations between zone of residence (Central, East, North, West, and South), epidemiological characteristics, and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B (anti-HBs) were evaluated by using univariable Poisson regression to estimate unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Consistent with established variable-selection procedures, variables with p-values < 0.20 in the univariable analyses were selected for inclusion in the multivariable Poisson regression model. Differences in demographic characteristics and cancer type across the five zones were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B, defined as immunity resulting from prior hepatitis B vaccination rather than previous infection, was considered present when anti-HBs was reactive and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) was non-reactive. All serological tests were performed using a chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) on the Alinity i system (Abbott Diagnostics, Chicago, IL, USA) at the Central Laboratory Division of HCFMUSP. According to the laboratory’s routine procedures, an anti-HBs titer ≥ 10 IU/L was classified as reactive. Testing was conducted as part of routine clinical care before the study began, with data subsequently retrieved from the hospital’s medical records. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSIn 2023, 2,792 adult cancer patients underwent anti-HBs serological testing at ICESP. Of these, 327 were excluded because anti-HBc testing had not been performed, 253 because they were anti-HBc-reactive, and 33 because they were HBsAg-reactive. Although 2,179 patients met the initial serological criteria, 1,036 were excluded because they resided outside Sao Paulo city. Consequently, the final study population comprised 1,143 patients who met all inclusion and exclusion criteria.Among included patients, the mean age was 57.4 ± 16.42 years, 61.9% were female, and 60.6% self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 76.8% of cases, whereas hematological malignancies accounted for 19.4%. Patients were distributed across all zones of the city, with the largest proportions residing in the South (29.7%) and East (25.0%) (Supplementary Table S1).Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Descriptively, the highest proportions were observed in the South (28.9%, 98/339) and East (28.7%, 82/286), whereas the lowest was observed in the North (20.7%, 51/246). The regional distribution and corresponding 95% CI are presented in Figure 1.In the univariable Poisson regression, serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B was less frequently observed among patients residing in the North than those residing in the South (20.7% versus 28.9%; PR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.51-1.01, p = 0.054).However, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders in the multivariable Poisson model (p = 0.139), indicating no independent association between zone of residence and serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. In contrast, age group and sex remained independently associated with the outcome (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Compared with patients aged ≥ 60 years, those aged 18-39 years were more likely to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (adjusted PR [aPR] = 3.56, 95% CI: 2.66-4.77), whereas patients aged 40-59 years were also more likely to present the outcome (aPR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.30-2.31). Likewise, female patients were more likely than male patients to present serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity (aPR = 1.42, 95% CI: 1.10-1.82).No statistically significant differences were observed in the distribution of age (p = 0.184), sex (p = 0.504), ethnicity/skin color (p = 0.835), or primary cancer type (p = 0.340) across the five zones of Sao Paulo city (Table 2). Descriptively, the West had the highest proportion of younger adults (18-39 years, 20.5%), whereas the North had the highest proportion of older adults (≥ 60 years, 55.3%). Female patients, White patients, and patients with solid tumors predominated across all regions. Likewise, despite slight descriptive variation in the proportion of patients with serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B across the five zones (Figure 1), no statistically significant regional differences were observed (p = 0.180). Several mechanisms may contribute to this finding, but they cannot be distinguished in this study. Older adults were less likely to have been vaccinated during childhood because universal hepatitis B vaccination for newborns was introduced in Brazil only in 1998, with expansion to all age groups occurring in 2015. Additionally, immunosenescence may reduce vaccine responsiveness and the persistence of detectable antibodies over time, as both innate and adaptive immune systems undergo progressive functional decline with aging 10 . Furthermore, among cancer patients, a lower frequency of detectable anti-HBs may also reflect waning antibodies, impaired immune responses related to the underlying malignancy or anticancer treatment, or a combination of these factors. Because information on vaccination history, timing of vaccination, and anticancer treatment was unavailable, these mechanisms could not be evaluated separately.Importantly, even among younger adults, serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity remained below expected levels. Previous Brazilian studies have similarly reported detectable anti-HBs in only 68.5% of vaccinated medical students 11 and 38.9% of children aged 1-15 years 12 , despite completion of the three-dose vaccination schedule. Furthermore, childhood hepatitis B vaccination coverage in Brazil was only 55.3% in 2021, remaining below the national target established by the Ministry of Health 13 .Sex-related differences were also observed. Women showed a higher frequency of serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B than men (29.9% versus 20.0%). This finding is consistent with previous reports showing stronger humoral responses to hepatitis B vaccination among women, including higher anti-HBs levels in healthcare workers 14 and a higher probability of vaccine non-response among men in Brazilian quilombola communities 15 . Biological differences in immune function, including hormonal influences, sex chromosome-related factors, and immune regulation, have been proposed as possible explanations for these observations 16 . Limited access to healthcare services, socioeconomic barriers, housing insecurity, and vaccine hesitancy have previously been associated with disparities in vaccination coverage in Sao Paulo city 17 and may also contribute to the observed patterns, although these factors were not evaluated in this study. Therefore, targeted strategies to improve hepatitis B vaccination and serological assessment among cancer patients remain warranted, particularly for older adults and men, who showed the lowest frequency of detectable anti-HBs. A recent systematic review showed that educational interventions, reminders, and patient counseling are effective strategies for improving vaccination uptake among patients with cancer 18 . Additionally, HBV screening before chemotherapy remains low worldwide, with a pooled rate of 57%, although screening rates have increased over time 19 . Expanding HBV screening and strengthening vaccination programs may help reduce the risk of HBV reactivation during anticancer treatment 20 .LimitationsThis study has several limitations. First, given the retrospective design, selection bias cannot be ruled out because information on the anti-HBs testing strategy was unavailable, and inclusion was restricted to patients with available HBV serological results. Second, information on socioeconomic and structural determinants was unavailable. Third, ethnicity/skin color was analyzed as a dichotomous variable (White versus non-White) because of the small number of participants in specific categories, which may have masked differences among individual racial and ethnic groups. Consequently, the serological profile evaluated in this study should be interpreted as evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity rather than as confirmation of vaccination. full_text_sections.conclusion: CONCLUSIONOnly 26.2% of cancer patients residing in Sao Paulo city presented serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Although regional differences were not statistically significant after adjustment, older adults and men were less likely to have serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity. These findings support the need to strengthen HBV screening and vaccination assessment in oncology care.

Within this context, preventive strategies are critical for patients with cancer, who are at increased risk of HBV reactivation and other infection-related complications driven by disease- and treatment-related immunosuppression 3 . In particular, anticancer therapies may predispose patients with previous HBV infection to viral reactivation and severe hepatic complications 3 .Vaccination against HBV is the primary strategy for preventing HBV infection in both the general population and patients receiving anticancer therapy. In the general population, seroprotection rates after completion of the full vaccination schedule are expected to reach 98%-100% in children and 90%-95% in adults. However, vaccine-induced immune responses are less robust among individuals older than 40-50 years 4 . The isolated presence of hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs), in the absence of anti-HBc, is widely accepted as serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. Additionally, documented vaccination records were unavailable, and no national system allows comprehensive retrieval of individual hepatitis B vaccination histories. Consequently, the serological profile evaluated in this study should be interpreted as evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity rather than as confirmation of vaccination. Finally, information regarding the timing of anti-HBs testing in relation to cancer diagnosis and anticancer treatment was unavailable. Therefore, it was not possible to distinguish whether low or undetectable anti-HBs levels reflected lack of vaccination, waning antibody levels over time, impaired vaccine response, treatment-related immunosuppression, or a combination of these mechanisms. Despite these limitations, the study provides important epidemiological data on serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity against hepatitis B among cancer patients and identifies demographic groups that may benefit from strengthened vaccination and testing strategies.

title_original: Regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil, addressing the need to understand how immunity varies across different geographic areas and populations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study was conducted among 1,143 adult cancer patients who underwent hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) testing at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) in 2023. The population included patients with solid tumors and hematological malignancies, with demographic and clinical characteristics retrieved from medical records.
analysis.methods: Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were used to identify associated factors, with variables selected based on p-values < 0.20 in univariable analyses. Associations between zone of residence and serological evidence were evaluated using Poisson regression to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
analysis.main_results: Overall, 26.2% (299/1,143) of cancer patients showed serological evidence compatible with vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B. The distribution across zones was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders, with no independent association found between zone of residence and anti-HBs status.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the regional distribution of vaccine-induced immunity did not show a significant association with zone of residence after adjusting for potential confounders, highlighting the need for targeted vaccination efforts in specific age groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that age-related differences in immunity to hepatitis B are significant, and may inform public health strategies to improve vaccination coverage in high-risk populations, particularly younger adults.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is strong due to the use of multivariable Poisson regression and a large sample size, with a moderate confidence assessment based on the statistical methods employed.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the regional distribution of serological evidence of vaccine-induced immunity to hepatitis B among cancer patients in a city in southeastern Brazil. A retrospective observational study of 1,143 patients was conducted, with data collected from medical records. Univariable and multivariable Poisson regression analyses were used to assess associations between zone of residence and immunity status. Overall, 26.2% of patients showed serological evidence of immunity, but no independent association with geographic region was found after adjustment. Age-related differences were observed, with younger adults more likely to have immunity. The study highlights the importance of targeted vaccination efforts, particularly in younger populations, to address disparities in hepatitis B immunity. The evidence is strong due to the statistical methods used, but the observational design limits causal conclusions.

full_text: AbstractObjectiveTo evaluate the association between receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care and depressive symptoms and medication adherence among patients with CHB receiving antiviral therapy.MethodsIn this retrospective cohort study, 200 patients diagnosed with CHB and treated at our hospital's hepatology clinic between July 2022 and June 2025 were included. Based on historical records, 100 patients who voluntarily completed a structured 12-week resilience promotion program in addition to standard care formed the observation group, and 100 patients who received standard care only formed the control group. Primary outcomes at the 6-month follow-up were depressive symptom severity measured by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and medication adherence measured by the Medication Possession Ratio (MPR). Secondary outcomes included resilience (Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10, CD-RISC-10), virological response, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalization, quality of life (SF-36), adverse events, and healthcare utilization. To account for potential confounding by indication and baseline imbalances, multivariable linear, logistic, and Poisson regression models were used, with adjusted effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals reported.ResultsAt the 6-month follow-up, the observation group had lower depression scores (6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 10.23 ± 4.12), higher MPR (0.92 ± 0.08 vs. 0.78 ± 0.15), and higher resilience scores (32.45 ± 5.67 vs. 26.78 ± 6.34). Virological response (85.0% vs. 70.0%; adjusted OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.48) and ALT normalization (80.0% vs. 65.0%; adjusted OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.10 to 3.67) were more frequent in the observation group. The program spanned 12 weeks, with one 90-minute session per week, co-facilitated by a certified clinical psychologist and a hepatology nurse specialist. Intervention modules included: (i) Psychoeducation: covering CHB disease knowledge, treatment goals, and the importance of long-term management, while addressing misconceptions; (ii) Cognitive Restructuring: identifying disease-related automatic negative thoughts (e.g., “the disease is incurable,” “I am a burden to my family”) and techniques to challenge and replace them; (iii) Stress and Emotion Management: training in relaxation techniques (e.g., progressive muscle relaxation), mindful breathing, and emotional labeling; (iv) Problem-Solving Skills Training: role-playing and discussion of solutions to adherence barriers (e.g., forgetfulness, side effect concerns); (v) Resilience Resource Building: guiding patients to explore and strengthen personal strengths, sense of value, and social support networks. Baseline (index date) was defined as the date of the first psychosocial screening record during the study period. For the observation group, the intervention period was the subsequent 12 weeks, and the 6-month follow-up outcome assessment was performed at 6 months after the index date (i.e., approximately 3 months after program completion). For the control group, there was no intervention period, and the 6-month follow-up outcome assessment was also performed at 6 months after the index date. Baseline PHQ-9, CD-RISC-10, SF-36, HBV DNA, and ALT values were incorporated into adjusted follow-up models using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) for continuous outcomes.2.3.3.Bias control strategiesBecause participation in the resilience program was voluntary, self-selection bias, confounding by indication, and completer bias are fundamental limitations. Patients who chose the intervention and completed all sessions may have had higher baseline motivation, better social support, and a greater propensity for adherence, which cannot be fully captured by measured covariates. To quantify baseline comparability, we calculated standardized differences for all baseline covariates; standardized differences <0.10 were considered negligible, and any covariates with standardized differences ≥0.10 were considered for adjustment regardless of P value. All adjusted estimates should be interpreted as associations conditional on observed variables, not as unbiased causal effects.Fibrosis stage was not systematically recorded; cirrhosis was identified from clinical documentation based on ultrasonography, transient elastography (where available), or FIB-4/APRI indices. Detailed antiviral treatment history (prior switches, interruptions) and quantitative HBsAg levels were not uniformly available in the electronic records and thus could not be included. This 9-item instrument is scored from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) per item, yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 27. Interpretation: 0–4 (none), 5–9 (mild), 10–14 (moderate), 15–19 (moderately severe), 20–27 (severe). Administered at baseline and 6 months post-intervention. MPR was defined as the total days’ supply of medication dispensed during the 6-month follow-up period divided by the number of days in the follow-up period (180 days). MPR values range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better adherence. MPR was analyzed as a continuous variable, and good adherence was defined a priori as MPR ≥ 0.80. ALT values were recorded at baseline and 6 months, and ALT normalization rate was calculated, defined as reduction to within the upper limit of normal (≤35 U/L for men, ≤25 U/L for women). This limitation is discussed later.2.4.6.Health-Related quality of lifeEvaluated using the Chinese version of the 36-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). This instrument comprises 8 domains, summarized into Physical Component Summary (PCS) and Mental Component Summary (MCS) scores; higher scores indicate better quality of life. Assessment timing aligned with the PHQ-9.2.4.7.Adverse events related to antiviral therapySystematically reviewed from patient complaints and physician diagnoses documented in medical records. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveTo evaluate the association between receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care and depressive symptoms and medication adherence among patients with CHB receiving antiviral therapy.MethodsIn this retrospective cohort study, 200 patients diagnosed with CHB and treated at our hospital's hepatology clinic between July 2022 and June 2025 were included. Based on historical records, 100 patients who voluntarily completed a structured 12-week resilience promotion program in addition to standard care formed the observation group, and 100 patients who received standard care only formed the control group. Primary outcomes at the 6-month follow-up were depressive symptom severity measured by the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and medication adherence measured by the Medication Possession Ratio (MPR). Secondary outcomes included resilience (Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10, CD-RISC-10), virological response, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) normalization, quality of life (SF-36), adverse events, and healthcare utilization. To account for potential confounding by indication and baseline imbalances, multivariable linear, logistic, and Poisson regression models were used, with adjusted effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals reported.ResultsAt the 6-month follow-up, the observation group had lower depression scores (6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 10.23 ± 4.12), higher MPR (0.92 ± 0.08 vs. 0.78 ± 0.15), and higher resilience scores (32.45 ± 5.67 vs. 26.78 ± 6.34). Virological response (85.0% vs. 70.0%; adjusted OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.48) and ALT normalization (80.0% vs. 65.0%; adjusted OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.10 to 3.67) were more frequent in the observation group. SF-36 physical and mental component scores were also higher in the observation group. Adverse event incidence was similar between groups. The observation group had fewer unplanned outpatient visits (P = 0.045), and Poisson regression confirmed fewer outpatient visits in the observation group (adjusted rate ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.93). However, because allocation was non-randomized, these associations may be affected by self-selection and residual confounding.ConclusionIn this retrospective cohort study, receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care was associated with lower depressive symptoms, better medication adherence, and more favorable virological and biochemical outcomes in patients with CHB.Keywords: chronic hepatitis B, depression, resilience intervention, retrospective study, treatment adherence

Initial screening identified 412 potentially eligible individuals. After sequential exclusions, a total of 200 patients were ultimately included in the analysis, with 100 assigned to the observation group and 100 to the control group. The primary reasons for exclusion comprised coexisting other liver diseases, missing key follow-up data, and receipt of professional psychotherapy at baseline. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis retrospective cohort study examined the association between receiving a structured resilience-based program in addition to standard care and depressive symptoms and medication adherence in patients undergoing antiviral therapy for CHB. The results showed that patients in the observation group had more favorable scores across several psychological, behavioral, virological, and biochemical domains. However, these are adjusted associations from non-randomized data and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality. The consistency across domains suggests that further prospective evaluation of such programs may be warranted, but the findings are hypothesis-generating (15, 16).Regarding psychological and behavioral outcomes, the observation group had lower depression scores, higher MPR, and higher resilience scores. These associations are biologically plausible but remain hypothetical. The program incorporated cognitive-behavioral techniques and positive psychology principles that may reduce disease-related automatic negative thoughts and improve self-management motivation, but these mechanisms were not directly measured. Skill-building components such as problem-solving and relaxation techniques may also facilitate behavioral change, but this interpretation is speculative. Previous studies have reported that similar psychological interventions are associated with reduced depression and improved adherence in chronic disease populations, although many focused on single outcomes. The present study extends these observations by examining multidimensional outcomes within CHB (17, 18).For virological and biochemical outcomes, the observation group had higher virological response and ALT normalization rates and greater reductions in HBV DNA and ALT. A possible explanation is that better medication adherence may have contributed to these differences, but this was not formally tested as a mediation pathway. Neuroendocrine and autonomic mechanisms linking psychological distress to immune control of HBV are plausible hypotheses, but were not evaluated because biomarkers such as cortisol and cytokines were not measured. Prior observational studies have reported associations between psychological factors and virological outcomes in HIV and HCV, but evidence in CHB remains limited. These findings should therefore be viewed as generating hypotheses for future mechanistic work (19, 20).Quality of life scores were higher in the observation group, and the incidence of adverse events was similar between groups. Although no safety concerns were observed, the statement that the program “can safely enhance” well-being would be too strong for an observational study. The observed difference in quality of life may reflect better emotional and functional adaptation, but this remains an association. Previous literature has reported improved quality of life after psychological interventions in cancer and cardiovascular disease; the present findings are consistent with those reports but require prospective confirmation in CHB (21, 22).The observation group had fewer unplanned outpatient visits, although the difference in emergency department visits or hospital admissions was not statistically significant. This may reflect better symptom management or reduced distress-driven healthcare seeking, but these explanations are speculative. The possibility that such programs could reduce healthcare utilization deserves further health-economic evaluation, but the present data are insufficient to support a cost-containment claim (23, 24).Multivariable regression analysis showed that receiving the resilience program was associated with more favorable outcomes after adjustment for measured confounders. However, these are adjusted associations, not independent effects. Residual confounding by unmeasured factors such as baseline motivation, social support, and personality traits cannot be excluded, and the retrospective design precludes causal inference. Future prospective randomized studies are needed to determine whether the observed associations reflect a true intervention effect or selection bias (25, 26).This study has several important limitations that should be carefully considered when interpreting the findings. First, the retrospective, non-randomized design and voluntary participation in the resilience program introduce substantial self-selection bias. Patients who chose to attend the intervention may have had higher intrinsic motivation, better social support, more adaptive personality traits, and a greater baseline propensity for adherence—characteristics that cannot be fully captured by measured covariates. Consequently, despite multivariable adjustment, residual confounding may substantially inflate the observed benefits, and no causal conclusions can be drawn. Second, the absence of randomization and the lack of propensity score matching or inverse probability weighting (not performed because of the modest sample size and the risk of model overfitting) further limit the ability to balance unmeasured confounders between groups. Third, the follow-up duration was only 6 months, which is insufficient to assess the sustainability of any psychological, behavioral, or virological improvements or to capture long-term endpoints such as HBsAg seroclearance or liver-related complications. Fourth, key hepatological covariates were incompletely captured: quantitative HBsAg levels, fibrosis stage assessed by biopsy or transient elastography, detailed treatment switch histories, and concurrent metabolic comorbidities such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease were not systematically recorded, which may introduce additional residual confounding. Fifth, uptake of external mental health care (e.g., private counseling, antidepressant pharmacotherapy) during follow-up was not monitored and could have influenced depression and adherence trajectories. Sixth, the study was conducted in a single Chinese center, and the sociodemographic and cultural characteristics of this cohort limit the generalizability of the findings to other populations and healthcare settings. Finally, multiple correlated outcomes were tested without multiplicity adjustment, increasing the risk of type I error, and given the sample size the regression models may be overfitted, so the reported effect estimates and confidence intervals should be interpreted with caution. These limitations underscore the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up, more comprehensive covariate measurement, and ideally multicenter recruitment to confirm or refute these exploratory findings.In conclusion, this retrospective study suggests that a structured resilience program is associated with more favorable psychological, behavioral, and clinical outcomes in CHB patients. Given the observational design and substantial risk of selection bias, these findings are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as evidence of efficacy. Well-designed randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up and biomarker assessments are needed before considering integration into routine care.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionChronic hepatitis B (CHB) represents a global public health challenge caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, with long-term persistence potentially leading to severe complications including liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (1). Antiviral therapy constitutes the cornerstone of CHB management; however, extended treatment duration, drug-related side effects, and psychosocial stressors frequently contribute to depressive symptoms and reduced treatment adherence among patients (2). Depression is highly prevalent in CHB populations, potentially linked to disease-related stress, immune-inflammatory responses, and neuroendocrine dysregulation (3). Suboptimal adherence directly undermines virological suppression, elevating risks of treatment failure and disease progression (4). Psychological interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and positive psychology approaches, have been employed in chronic disease management to enhance psychological resilience and self-management capabilities (5). Resilience refers to an individual's capacity to maintain psychological adaptation and positive adjustment in the face of adversity, with levels inversely correlated with depression and positively associated with adherence (6). Previous studies indicate that resilience-based interventions can improve psychological and behavioral outcomes in patients with chronic conditions such as cancer and diabetes; however, evidence within CHB populations remains limited, often focusing on single dimensions such as mood or adherence, and lacking comprehensive multi-dimensional assessment (7).Although randomized controlled trials provide the strongest evidence for efficacy, their controlled conditions may not fully reflect real-world uptake and outcomes. Observational data from clinical practice can complement these trials by describing implementation patterns and adjusted associations in unselected patient populations (8). Standard care in CHB typically provides medication instructions and brief adherence counseling but lacks structured psychological components to manage disease-related automatic negative thoughts, stigma, and emotional distress—factors associated with non-adherence (9). A resilience-based program targets these cognitive-emotional barriers and may be associated with outcomes not achieved through conventional education alone (10). However, because participation in such programs is typically voluntary in clinical practice, patients who choose to participate may differ systematically from those who do not. This non-random exposure introduces selection bias, confounding by indication, and residual confounding by unmeasured factors such as baseline motivation, social support, and adherence propensity. In the present study, the resilience program was offered to all eligible CHB patients, but uptake was voluntary and depended on patient preference, perceived need, and scheduling availability. These differences cannot be fully captured by measured covariates, and all observed associations should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Several studies in this area have also been limited by short follow-up and incomplete adjustment for baseline clinical and sociodemographic factors (11, 12). Furthermore, biological mechanisms involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, cortisol, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α have been proposed to link psychological distress with impaired immune control of HBV (13, 14); however, these biomarkers were not measured in the present study, and these pathways remain theoretical.This study leverages a retrospective cohort design to explore real-world associations between a structured resilience program and multidimensional outcomes in CHB. Although the observational nature precludes causal inference, the inclusion of psychological, behavioral, virological, and healthcare utilization endpoints, together with multivariable adjustment, allows a more integrated description of potential benefits and limitations of such interventions. The findings are intended to generate hypotheses and inform the design of future prospective trials, rather than to validate intervention efficacy. 2.1.Study populationThis retrospective cohort study utilized data extracted from the electronic medical record system of our hospital's hepatology clinic. A total of 200 patients diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and receiving antiviral therapy between July 2022 to June 2025 were included. Based on historical records, 100 patients who voluntarily and regularly completed a systematic “Resilience Promotion Program” in addition to routine treatment were assigned to the observation group; the remaining 100 patients received standard care only and were designated as the control group. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of both groups, retrieved and summarized in Table 1 (presented in the Results section), indicated that the group distribution reflected the natural proportion of eligible patients receiving structured psychological intervention in real-world practice. The observation group comprised 59 males and 41 females, with a mean age of 44.01 ± 12.32 years; the control group included 66 males and 34 females, with a mean age of 46.53 ± 13.97 years. The Resilience Promotion Program was an optional, clinic-based service offered to all CHB patients; participation was voluntary and not part of standard medical care. The PHQ-9 was administered to all patients as part of routine psychosocial screening during nurse-led education sessions. title_original: Depression and medication adherence among chronic hepatitis B patients receiving resilience-based care versus standard care during antiviral therapy: a retrospective cohort study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the association between receiving a resilience-focused program in addition to standard care and depressive symptoms and medication adherence among patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) undergoing antiviral therapy. This is important because depression and poor medication adherence can negatively impact treatment outcomes in CHB patients.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective cohort study included 200 patients diagnosed with CHB and treated at the hepatology clinic between July 2022 and June 2025. Patients were divided into two groups: 100 who completed a 12-week resilience promotion program and 100 who received standard care only.
analysis.methods: Multivariable regression models were used to adjust for potential confounding factors, incorporating baseline PHQ-9, CD-RISC-10, SF-36, HBV DNA, and ALT values. Medication adherence was assessed using the Medication Possession Ratio (MPR) from pharmacy refill records, and statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 26.0 and R 4.3.1.
analysis.main_results: At the 6-month follow-up, the observation group had lower depression scores (6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 9.21 ± 4.12) and fewer unplanned outpatient visits (adjusted rate ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.93). However, the study acknowledges potential biases due to non-randomized allocation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the resilience-focused program may contribute to improved depressive symptoms and medication adherence, which could lead to more favorable virological and biochemical outcomes. This is a novel finding as it highlights the potential benefits of integrating psychological support into CHB treatment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that resilience-based care could be a valuable addition to standard treatment for CHB, potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare utilization. This has implications for enhancing patient support strategies in clinical practice.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by non-randomized allocation, which may introduce self-selection bias and residual confounding. Despite these limitations, the evidence is moderate due to the use of adjusted models and complete-case analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study investigated the impact of resilience-based care on depressive symptoms and medication adherence in patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) undergoing antiviral therapy. The study included 200 patients, with 100 receiving a structured 12-week resilience program and 100 receiving standard care. Results showed lower depression scores and fewer unplanned outpatient visits in the resilience group, though non-randomized allocation raises concerns about self-selection bias. The authors suggest that resilience-based care may improve outcomes, offering a novel approach to CHB management. The study's moderate evidence strength is due to its design limitations and the use of adjusted models. These findings could inform future strategies for integrating psychological support into CHB treatment, potentially enhancing patient adherence and reducing healthcare burden.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估接受 抗病毒药物 治疗的 慢性乙型肝炎 (CHB) 患者在标准护理之外接受以恢复力为中心的计划与抑郁症状和药物依从性之间的关系。这很重要,因为抑郁症和药物依从性差会对慢性乙型肝炎患者的 治疗 结果产生负面影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项回顾性 队列研究 研究纳入了 2022 年 7 月至 2025 年 6 月期间诊断为慢性乙型肝炎并在肝病诊所接受治疗的 200 名患者。患者被分为两组:100 名完成了 12 周的恢复力促进计划的患者和 100 名仅接受标准护理的患者。
elements_zh.methods: 使用多变量回归模型来调整潜在的混杂因素,纳入基线 PHQ-9、CD-RISC-10、SF-36、HBV DNA 和 ALT 值。使用药房补充记录中的药物持有率(MPR)评估用药依从性,并使用 SPSS 26.0 和 R 4.3.1 进行统计分析。
elements_zh.main_results: At the 6-month follow-up, the observation group had lower depression scores (6.78 ± 3.45 vs. 9.21 ± 4.12) and fewer unplanned outpatient visits (adjusted rate ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.93). However, the study acknowledges potential biases due to non-randomized allocation.
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,以恢复力为重点的计划可能有助于改善抑郁症状和药物依从性,从而带来更有利的病毒学和生化结果。这是一个新颖的发现,因为它强调了将心理支持纳入 CHB 治疗 的潜在好处。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,基于复原力的护理可能是慢性乙型肝炎标准 治疗 的一个有价值的补充,有可能改善患者的治疗结果并减少医疗保健的利用率。这对于加强临床实践中的患者支持策略具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到非随机分配的限制,这可能会引入自选择偏差和残余混杂。尽管存在这些局限性,但由于使用了调整模型和完整案例分析,证据是中等的。

analysis_zh.methods: 使用多变量回归模型来调整潜在的混杂因素,纳入基线 PHQ-9、CD-RISC-10、SF-36、HBV DNA 和 ALT 值。使用药房补充记录中的药物持有率(MPR)评估用药依从性,并使用 SPSS 26.0 和 R 4.3.1 进行统计分析。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,以恢复力为重点的计划可能有助于改善抑郁症状和药物依从性,从而带来更有利的病毒学和生化结果。这是一个新颖的发现,因为它强调了将心理支持纳入 CHB 治疗 的潜在好处。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,基于复原力的护理可能是慢性乙型肝炎标准 治疗 的一个有价值的补充,有可能改善患者的治疗结果并减少医疗保健的利用率。这对于加强临床实践中的患者支持策略具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到非随机分配的限制,这可能会引入自选择偏差和残余混杂。尽管存在这些局限性,但由于使用了调整模型和完整案例分析,证据是中等的。

title: Plasma exchange and double plasma molecular adsorption system combined with continuous renal replacement therapy for hepatitis B-related liver failure complicated by stage 3 acute kidney injury: a case report

full_text: AbstractBackgroundHepatitis B virus (HBV)-related liver failure can progress rapidly to neurological and renal dysfunction. In this setting, declining aminotransferase levels may be misleading if hepatic synthetic function and extrahepatic organ function continue to deteriorate.Case presentationA 27-year-old woman presented with severe fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice. Laboratory testing showed marked hepatocellular injury, coagulopathy, HBV infection markers, and an HBV DNA level of 3.57 × 106 copies/mL. During hospitalization, serum aminotransferase levels declined substantially; however, bilirubin and coagulation abnormalities worsened, serum creatinine increased from 96 μmol/L on day 1 to 825 μmol/L on day 4, and the patient developed hypersomnia and impaired consciousness. The renal deterioration met criteria for stage 3 acute kidney injury. Following multidisciplinary assessment, plasma exchange combined with a double plasma molecular adsorption system was used for liver-directed extracorporeal support, while continuous renal replacement therapy was initiated primarily for severe acute kidney injury and metabolic support. Consciousness, coagulation, liver function, and renal function subsequently improved. The patient left the intensive care unit on day 7, was discharged on day 24, and maintained normal liver and kidney function during follow-up.ConclusionThis case highlights that declining aminotransferase levels do not necessarily indicate clinical recovery in rapidly progressive HBV-related liver failure. Serial assessment of hepatic synthetic function, neurological status, and renal function identified continued multiorgan deterioration and guided timely, indication-based extracorporeal support. The clinical value of this case lies in the decision-making process for coordinated liver and renal support rather than in the novelty of the individual treatment modalities.Keywords: acute kidney injury, continuous renal replacement therapy, double plasma molecular adsorption system, hepatitis B-related liver failure, plasma exchange 3.DiscussionThe principal clinical contribution of this case is the demonstration of a decision-making process in which longitudinal, multi-organ function assessment guided the sequential and coordinated use of multimodal extracorporeal therapies in a patient with HBV-related liver failure and stage 3 AKI. The marked discordance between declining aminotransferase levels and worsening synthetic function, coagulopathy, neurological status, and renal function signaled progression to multi-organ failure, rather than recovery. Recognizing this trajectory prompted a multidisciplinary reassessment that led to an indication-based strategy: PE/DPMAS for liver-directed support and CRRT primarily for severe AKI and metabolic management. This case illustrates how dynamic, multi-organ assessment, rather than reliance on any single laboratory parameter, is critical for the timely escalation and appropriate selection of complementary organ-support modalities.This patient had no known history of chronic viral hepatitis and no family history of chronic viral hepatitis. During this period of hospitalization, she tested positive for hepatitis B surface antigen and exhibited a high level of HBV DNA. Other potential causes of hepatitis and liver injury, such as additional viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver damage, metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, autoimmune hepatic conditions, and drug-induced hepatotoxicity, were thoroughly considered and subsequently excluded based on comprehensive history-taking and laboratory assessment. These findings are compatible with a recent HBV infection but do not, by themselves, definitively distinguish primary acute hepatitis B from previously unrecognized chronic HBV infection with acute exacerbation. In particular, the available case data did not include a quantitative IgM anti-HBc result or documented previous HBsAg-negative testing that could establish recent acquisition of HBV with greater confidence. At the time the patient's clinical condition stabilized (with normalized vital signs and controlled encephalopathy), we were faced with a fundamental management decision: whether this was Acute Hepatitis B (AVH-B) with spontaneous clearance potential, or Acute-on-Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB-AE) with underlying cirrhosis/fibrosis. These two entities dictate completely different long-term strategies regarding antiviral therapy duration, discontinuation timing, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance frequency. Serum markers alone (HBV-DNA, IgM anti-HBc) were unable to definitively differentiate between the two, as high-level viremia and positive IgM can occur in both scenarios. Therefore, liver histology was pursued as the gold standard to guide long-term prognosis, rather than to evaluate the immediate recovery from acute failure.AKI is a relatively common complication of hepatitis B-related liver failure. In a large-scale retrospective cohort study that enrolled 86,204 patients with HBV infection without baseline cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma, 4,407 (5.1%) patients were found to have experienced AKI (3). The development of severe AKI necessitates rapid multidisciplinary intervention. While CRRT was initiated in this patient primarily for stage 3 AKI, its potential benefits in the context of liver failure extend beyond renal replacement. Emerging evidence and guidelines suggest that CRRT can be employed to manage hyperammonemia and hepatic encephalopathy, even in the absence of conventional renal replacement therapy indications (3–5). In this case, CRRT contributed to the control of fluid balance, electrolytes, and acid-base status, and may have also assisted in managing the metabolic consequences of liver failure. This highlights that the clinical effects of CRRT are multi-faceted, although its principal indication in this patient remained renal support.Hepatitis B-related liver failure is a critical illness with an acute onset, rapid progression, and high mortality (6). Due to the clinical progression, which may advance rapidly, a significant number of patients loses the opportunity for timely liver transplantation. With advancements in intensive care and emergency liver transplantation, the mortality rate of Hepatitis B-related liver failure has decreased (7). Artificial liver support is an important supportive strategy in treating Hepatitis B-related liver failure. Commonly utilized systems comprise the Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS) and the Plasma Separation and Adsorption System (SEPAD) (8, 9). In China, PE is a common non-bioartificial liver support therapy that removes toxins related to liver failure and supplies active substances, including coagulation factors and albumin. However, PE alone has a limited ability to clear inflammatory mediators, creatinine, and other small-molecule toxins. DPMAS connects a bilirubin adsorber and resin perfusion device to the plasma circuit. It can adsorb bilirubin and bile acids and may also remove endotoxin and inflammatory mediators while reducing plasma consumption (10).In this case, the treatment effects of PE, DPMAS, and CRRT were complementary. DPMAS may have contributed to bilirubin, bile acid, endotoxin, and inflammatory mediator removal. PE may have compensated for the loss of beneficial plasma components, such as coagulation factors and growth factors, and may have supported liver regeneration (11). In this patient, the combination was therefore used as an individualized liver-support strategy addressing both toxin removal and plasma-component replacement. Nevertheless, because PE and DPMAS were administered together, the clinical contribution of each component cannot be separated in this single case.The principal clinical lesson from this case is the value of systematic, longitudinal assessment of multiple organ systems—rather than reliance on a single laboratory trend—in guiding the timely escalation and appropriate selection of complementary extracorporeal therapies. In this patient, the discordant improvement in transaminase levels alongside worsening synthetic, neurological, and renal function prompted a multidisciplinary reassessment, leading to a coordinated strategy: PE/DPMAS for liver-directed support and CRRT for stage 3 AKI. Although the subsequent recovery was temporally associated with this approach, a single case cannot establish causality or determine the independent contribution of each modality. 1.IntroductionHepatitis B virus (HBV)-related liver failure is a critical syndrome characterised by acute hepatic decompensation and frequently leads to multiorgan failure, with a high short-term mortality rate (1). Among the various complications, Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequently observed and prognostically important complication in patients with HBV-related liver failure (2). The development of AKI significantly worsens patient prognosis, and higher AKI stages are associated with substantially increased short-term mortality (3). Although plasma exchange, plasma adsorption, and continuous renal replacement therapy are established extracorporeal interventions, a practical challenge is determining when organ support should be escalated and which modality should be selected for each component of multiorgan dysfunction. Here, We report a case of HBV-related liver failure presenting with a marked decrease in aminotransferase levels, along with progressive coagulopathy, hyperbilirubinemia, neurological deterioration, and stage 3 acute kidney injury. This case illustrates the importance of longitudinal multiorgan assessment and indication-based coordination of extracorporeal liver and renal support. 2.Case presentationA 27-year-old woman presented to a local hospital with profound fatigue and dark urine for 2 days. She had donated blood several times, and had no known history of hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection. Her close relatives had no history of chronic viral hepatitis. On admission, her blood pressure was 101/62 mmHg, and her pulse rate was 72 beats/min. Physical examination showed jaundice of the skin and sclerae, with right upper abdominal tenderness and rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests revealed severe hepatocellular injury and coagulopathy (Table 1). PE may have compensated for the loss of beneficial plasma components, such as coagulation factors and growth factors, and may have supported liver regeneration (11). In this patient, the combination was therefore used as an individualized liver-support strategy addressing both toxin removal and plasma-component replacement. Nevertheless, because PE and DPMAS were administered together, the clinical contribution of each component cannot be separated in this single case.The principal clinical lesson from this case is the value of systematic, longitudinal assessment of multiple organ systems—rather than reliance on a single laboratory trend—in guiding the timely escalation and appropriate selection of complementary extracorporeal therapies. In this patient, the discordant improvement in transaminase levels alongside worsening synthetic, neurological, and renal function prompted a multidisciplinary reassessment, leading to a coordinated strategy: PE/DPMAS for liver-directed support and CRRT for stage 3 AKI. Although the subsequent recovery was temporally associated with this approach, a single case cannot establish causality or determine the independent contribution of each modality.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionHepatitis B virus (HBV)-related liver failure is a critical syndrome characterised by acute hepatic decompensation and frequently leads to multiorgan failure, with a high short-term mortality rate (1). Among the various complications, Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequently observed and prognostically important complication in patients with HBV-related liver failure (2). The development of AKI significantly worsens patient prognosis, and higher AKI stages are associated with substantially increased short-term mortality (3). Although plasma exchange, plasma adsorption, and continuous renal replacement therapy are established extracorporeal interventions, a practical challenge is determining when organ support should be escalated and which modality should be selected for each component of multiorgan dysfunction. Here, We report a case of HBV-related liver failure presenting with a marked decrease in aminotransferase levels, along with progressive coagulopathy, hyperbilirubinemia, neurological deterioration, and stage 3 acute kidney injury. This case illustrates the importance of longitudinal multiorgan assessment and indication-based coordination of extracorporeal liver and renal support. 2.Case presentationA 27-year-old woman presented to a local hospital with profound fatigue and dark urine for 2 days. She had donated blood several times, and had no known history of hepatitis B or hepatitis C infection. Her close relatives had no history of chronic viral hepatitis. On admission, her blood pressure was 101/62 mmHg, and her pulse rate was 72 beats/min. Physical examination showed jaundice of the skin and sclerae, with right upper abdominal tenderness and rebound tenderness.
