full_text: AbstractIntroductionThe prognostic relevance of baseline low-level viremia (LLV) after hepatitis B virus-related hepatocellular carcinoma (HBV-HCC) diagnosis remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between baseline LLV and overall survival (OS), explored related biological features, and developed survival prediction models for patients with baseline LLV.MethodsThis retrospective study included 921 patients with HBV-HCC: 611 with baseline LLV and 310 with HBV DNA <20 IU/mL. Propensity score matching (PSM), inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and Cox regression were used to assess the association between baseline HBV DNA status and OS. Peripheral T cell subsets and selected markers of hepatic functional reserve, hepatocellular injury, and systemic inflammation were explored. Patients with baseline LLV were randomly divided into training and reserved internal validation sets. Model 1 used the full candidate variable set, whereas Model 2 used non-imaging variables. Predictors were selected using LASSO Cox regression and Boruta, and five survival algorithms were compared within the training set.ResultsBaseline LLV was associated with poorer OS. After PSM, HBV DNA <20 IU/mL was associated with lower adjusted mortality than LLV (hazard ratio, 0.688; 95% confidence interval, 0.543–0.872; P = 0.002), with similar findings after IPTW. Patients with LLV had a lower peripheral CD4/CD8 ratio, and exploratory analyses identified significant indirect associations through albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, and systemic immune-inflammation response index. Model 1 retained tumor size, tumor multiplicity, portal vein tumor thrombus, cholinesterase, alkaline phosphatase, and alpha-fetoprotein; Model 2 retained gamma-glutamyl transferase, cholinesterase, alkaline phosphatase, and alpha-fetoprotein. Random survival forest was selected based on overall training performance. In the reserved validation set, the 1-, 3-, and 5-year time-dependent AUCs were 0.824, 0.777, and 0.765 for Model 1 and 0.769, 0.742, and 0.723 for Model 2, respectively. Both models showed good calibration and positive net benefit.DiscussionBaseline LLV remained prognostically relevant after HCC diagnosis and was accompanied by exploratory differences in systemic inflammation and the relative balance of peripheral T cell subsets. These findings support closer virological monitoring and individualized risk assessment.Keywords: hepatitis B virus, hepatocellular carcinoma, low-level viremia, machine learning, overall survival MethodsStudy design and participantsThis retrospective study included patients diagnosed with HBV-HCC at Beijing Ditan Hospital between January 2007 and September 2017. Patients were categorized into two groups according to baseline HBV DNA level: the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group and the baseline LLV group, defined as HBV DNA 20–2000 IU/mL. Patients were excluded if they had HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection or other hepatotropic virus co-infection, other primary malignancies, baseline HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, or were lost to follow-up (Figure 1). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee.Figure 1Study flowchart of patient selection, survival analyses, and prediction model development.Flowchart detailing patient selection, survival analysis, and model development for HBV-HCC patients at Beijing Ditan Hospital, including exclusion criteria, division into cohorts, statistical analyses (KM, Cox, subgroup), feature selection, algorithm training, validation, SHAP analysis, and risk calculator creation.Outcome definition and follow-upOverall survival (OS) was defined as the interval from the date of initial HCC diagnosis to death from any cause. Vital status and dates of death were ascertained from electronic medical records, outpatient follow-up records, and telephone follow-up with patients or their family members. The administrative end of follow-up was September 2022. Median follow-up duration was estimated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method.Baseline data and missing data handlingClinical and laboratory variables were obtained from the evaluation associated with the baseline HBV DNA measurement. Study variables were selected according to clinical relevance, availability in routine practice, and previously reported prognostic value in HBV-HCC. Their definitions, classifications, cutoff values, and roles in the analyses are provided in Supplementary Table S1.Variables with less than 15% missingness were eligible for the primary analyses, whereas variables with greater missingness were considered only in exploratory analyses. The distribution of missing data is shown in Supplementary Figure S1. For analyses evaluating the association between baseline HBV DNA status and OS, missing baseline covariate values were imputed using a random forest-based method in the full cohort of 921 patients before propensity score and survival analyses. For prediction modeling, missing data were handled only after patients had been divided into the training and validation sets.Survival analysis and propensity score adjustmentTo reduce baseline imbalance between the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group and the baseline LLV group, propensity score matching (PSM) and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) were performed. Propensity scores were estimated using a logistic regression model that included prespecified baseline covariates selected for propensity score adjustment, as detailed in Supplementary Table S1. For PSM, patients were matched at a 1:1 ratio using nearest-neighbor matching without replacement and a caliper width equal to 0.1 times the standard deviation of the estimated propensity score distance. Propensity score overlap and covariate balance were evaluated before and after adjustment. An absolute standardized mean difference <0.10 was considered indicative of acceptable balance.Kaplan–Meier curves were generated to compare OS between groups in the unmatched and PSM cohorts, and differences were evaluated using the log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards models were fitted in the unmatched, propensity score-matched, and IPTW-weighted cohorts. Cluster-robust standard errors based on matched-pair membership were used for the PSM analyses, and robust sandwich variance estimates were used for the IPTW analyses. The multivariable models adjusted for prespecified clinical, virological, liver-related, and tumor-related factors.Multicollinearity and the proportional hazards assumption were evaluated as model diagnostics. Initial HCC treatment was defined as the first HCC-directed treatment modality recorded during the initial treatment course. All initial HCC treatments occurred after baseline HBV DNA measurement. Because treatment modality was therefore not a strict pre-exposure covariate and a potential mediating role could not be excluded, propensity score and multivariable analyses were repeated after excluding initial HCC treatment as a sensitivity analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed in the matched cohort, and interaction terms were used to examine heterogeneity across clinically relevant strata.Prediction model development and evaluationPrediction models were developed among patients with baseline LLV. Before any data processing for model development, patients were randomly divided in a 7:3 ratio into a training set and a held-out internal validation set. All decisions regarding data processing, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, and algorithm selection were based only on the training set.The random forest imputation procedure was fitted using the training data and then applied to the validation data without refitting. The cutoff for baseline HBV DNA within the LLV cohort was determined using X-tile in the training set and then applied unchanged to the validation set.Two prediction models were developed. Model 1 was derived from the full candidate variable set. Model 2 was derived from a non-imaging candidate variable set that excluded imaging-derived tumor characteristics and was designed as a simplified alternative for settings in which detailed imaging-derived tumor variables are incomplete or difficult to standardize. Feature selection for both models was conducted in the training set using Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression with 10-fold cross-validation and the Boruta algorithm. Variables retained by both approaches were used for model development.Using the selected predictors, five survival modeling algorithms were implemented for each model: Cox proportional hazards model, gradient boosting machine (GBM), support vector machine (SVM), random survival forest (RSF), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Model fitting, hyperparameter tuning, and algorithm comparison were performed only in the training set. The final algorithm was selected based on the overall balance of discrimination and prediction error across the prespecified evaluation time points in the training set. All model-development decisions were completed before the validation set was evaluated. The candidate parameter ranges, selected settings, random seed, and software specifications are provided in Supplementary Table S2.After model selection, the final models were fitted using the full training set and evaluated in the held-out validation set. The validation set did not contribute to data processing, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, algorithm selection, or any other development decision.Discrimination and prediction error were evaluated at 12, 36, and 60 months using time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and Brier scores. Corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Calibration was evaluated using calibration curves, and potential clinical utility was assessed using decision curve analysis. The final models were also compared with established prognostic systems.Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) after the final algorithm had been selected. SHAP values were calculated for the native prediction output of the selected survival model. Web-based risk calculators were subsequently constructed using the Shiny platform to estimate individualized 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities.Exploratory analysesExploratory analyses included evaluation of model performance across initial HCC treatment groups, mediation analyses of selected markers reflecting hepatic functional reserve, hepatocellular injury, and systemic inflammation, and analyses of available peripheral blood T cell subsets data. The immune analysis assessed the comparability of patients with and without available peripheral T cell subsets and compared selected peripheral blood T cell subsets parameters according to baseline HBV DNA status.General statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median with interquartile range, depending on their distribution, and were compared using Student’s t test or the Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages and compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. All analyses were performed using R software, version 4.0.5. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Study design and participantsThis retrospective study included patients diagnosed with HBV-HCC at Beijing Ditan Hospital between January 2007 and September 2017. Patients were categorized into two groups according to baseline HBV DNA level: the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group and the baseline LLV group, defined as HBV DNA 20–2000 IU/mL. Patients were excluded if they had HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection or other hepatotropic virus co-infection, other primary malignancies, baseline HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, or were lost to follow-up (Figure 1). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee.Figure 1Study flowchart of patient selection, survival analyses, and prediction model development.Flowchart detailing patient selection, survival analysis, and model development for HBV-HCC patients at Beijing Ditan Hospital, including exclusion criteria, division into cohorts, statistical analyses (KM, Cox, subgroup), feature selection, algorithm training, validation, SHAP analysis, and risk calculator creation. Of these, 611 were included in the baseline LLV group and 310 in the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group. full_text_sections.methods: MethodsStudy design and participantsThis retrospective study included patients diagnosed with HBV-HCC at Beijing Ditan Hospital between January 2007 and September 2017. Patients were categorized into two groups according to baseline HBV DNA level: the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group and the baseline LLV group, defined as HBV DNA 20–2000 IU/mL. Patients were excluded if they had HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection or other hepatotropic virus co-infection, other primary malignancies, baseline HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, or were lost to follow-up (Figure 1). The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee.Figure 1Study flowchart of patient selection, survival analyses, and prediction model development.Flowchart detailing patient selection, survival analysis, and model development for HBV-HCC patients at Beijing Ditan Hospital, including exclusion criteria, division into cohorts, statistical analyses (KM, Cox, subgroup), feature selection, algorithm training, validation, SHAP analysis, and risk calculator creation.Outcome definition and follow-upOverall survival (OS) was defined as the interval from the date of initial HCC diagnosis to death from any cause. Vital status and dates of death were ascertained from electronic medical records, outpatient follow-up records, and telephone follow-up with patients or their family members. The administrative end of follow-up was September 2022. Median follow-up duration was estimated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method.Baseline data and missing data handlingClinical and laboratory variables were obtained from the evaluation associated with the baseline HBV DNA measurement. Study variables were selected according to clinical relevance, availability in routine practice, and previously reported prognostic value in HBV-HCC. Their definitions, classifications, cutoff values, and roles in the analyses are provided in Supplementary Table S1.Variables with less than 15% missingness were eligible for the primary analyses, whereas variables with greater missingness were considered only in exploratory analyses. The distribution of missing data is shown in Supplementary Figure S1. For analyses evaluating the association between baseline HBV DNA status and OS, missing baseline covariate values were imputed using a random forest-based method in the full cohort of 921 patients before propensity score and survival analyses. For prediction modeling, missing data were handled only after patients had been divided into the training and validation sets.Survival analysis and propensity score adjustmentTo reduce baseline imbalance between the baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL group and the baseline LLV group, propensity score matching (PSM) and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) were performed. Propensity scores were estimated using a logistic regression model that included prespecified baseline covariates selected for propensity score adjustment, as detailed in Supplementary Table S1. For PSM, patients were matched at a 1:1 ratio using nearest-neighbor matching without replacement and a caliper width equal to 0.1 times the standard deviation of the estimated propensity score distance. Propensity score overlap and covariate balance were evaluated before and after adjustment. An absolute standardized mean difference <0.10 was considered indicative of acceptable balance.Kaplan–Meier curves were generated to compare OS between groups in the unmatched and PSM cohorts, and differences were evaluated using the log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards models were fitted in the unmatched, propensity score-matched, and IPTW-weighted cohorts. Cluster-robust standard errors based on matched-pair membership were used for the PSM analyses, and robust sandwich variance estimates were used for the IPTW analyses. The multivariable models adjusted for prespecified clinical, virological, liver-related, and tumor-related factors.Multicollinearity and the proportional hazards assumption were evaluated as model diagnostics. Initial HCC treatment was defined as the first HCC-directed treatment modality recorded during the initial treatment course. All initial HCC treatments occurred after baseline HBV DNA measurement. Because treatment modality was therefore not a strict pre-exposure covariate and a potential mediating role could not be excluded, propensity score and multivariable analyses were repeated after excluding initial HCC treatment as a sensitivity analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed in the matched cohort, and interaction terms were used to examine heterogeneity across clinically relevant strata.Prediction model development and evaluationPrediction models were developed among patients with baseline LLV. Before any data processing for model development, patients were randomly divided in a 7:3 ratio into a training set and a held-out internal validation set. All decisions regarding data processing, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, and algorithm selection were based only on the training set.The random forest imputation procedure was fitted using the training data and then applied to the validation data without refitting. The cutoff for baseline HBV DNA within the LLV cohort was determined using X-tile in the training set and then applied unchanged to the validation set.Two prediction models were developed. Model 1 was derived from the full candidate variable set. Model 2 was derived from a non-imaging candidate variable set that excluded imaging-derived tumor characteristics and was designed as a simplified alternative for settings in which detailed imaging-derived tumor variables are incomplete or difficult to standardize. Feature selection for both models was conducted in the training set using Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression with 10-fold cross-validation and the Boruta algorithm. Variables retained by both approaches were used for model development.Using the selected predictors, five survival modeling algorithms were implemented for each model: Cox proportional hazards model, gradient boosting machine (GBM), support vector machine (SVM), random survival forest (RSF), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Model fitting, hyperparameter tuning, and algorithm comparison were performed only in the training set. The final algorithm was selected based on the overall balance of discrimination and prediction error across the prespecified evaluation time points in the training set. All model-development decisions were completed before the validation set was evaluated. The candidate parameter ranges, selected settings, random seed, and software specifications are provided in Supplementary Table S2.After model selection, the final models were fitted using the full training set and evaluated in the held-out validation set. The validation set did not contribute to data processing, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, algorithm selection, or any other development decision.Discrimination and prediction error were evaluated at 12, 36, and 60 months using time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and Brier scores. Corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Calibration was evaluated using calibration curves, and potential clinical utility was assessed using decision curve analysis. The final models were also compared with established prognostic systems.Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) after the final algorithm had been selected. SHAP values were calculated for the native prediction output of the selected survival model. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis study has three main findings. First, baseline LLV was associated with poorer OS than baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL in patients with HBV-HCC. The association remained evident in the unmatched, PSM, and IPTW analyses. Second, exploratory immune analyses showed a lower peripheral CD4/CD8 ratio in patients with baseline LLV, whereas absolute CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts were similar between the two virological groups. Third, because patients with baseline LLV remained clinically heterogeneous, we developed two survival prediction models to refine individualized risk assessment within this population.Previous studies of LLV have focused predominantly on HCC development rather than prognosis after HCC diagnosis (9–11, 20). Evidence in patients with established HCC remains limited, and existing studies have often been restricted to specific treatment settings or have emphasized longitudinal HBV DNA patterns during follow-up (12–15). Because baseline HBV DNA is routinely available before or at the initiation of HCC treatment, it may provide a practical early marker for risk assessment before longitudinal virological data become available. By focusing on baseline HBV DNA status at initial HCC evaluation, our study therefore extends prior work from HCC risk prediction to post-diagnosis survival in patients with established HCC.Several mechanisms may explain the association between baseline LLV and poorer survival after HCC diagnosis. Persistent low-level HBV replication can sustain hepatic necroinflammation and hepatocyte injury, potentially accelerating deterioration of hepatic functional reserve (21, 22). In patients with HCC, impaired liver reserve may reduce treatment tolerance, limit eligibility for repeated or intensive antitumor therapies, and compromise post-treatment recovery (17, 23). Detectable HBV DNA at baseline may also indicate incomplete viral suppression and greater susceptibility to virological fluctuation or HBV reactivation during antitumor treatment (24–26). Consistent with this biological framework, our exploratory pathway analyses identified statistically significant indirect effects through ALB and AST, with estimated mediated proportions of 13.4% and 23.1%, respectively, whereas the indirect effects through CHE and ALT were not statistically significant. These findings support the possibility that hepatic functional impairment and hepatocellular injury contribute to the association between residual viral activity and survival. This pathway may be particularly relevant in patients whose prognosis is not overwhelmingly dominated by advanced tumor burden.Persistent viral activity may also influence systemic inflammation and host immune regulation. In patients with unresectable HBV-HCC receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, LLV has been associated with poorer treatment response and survival, and proteomic analysis identified differential expression of Flt3L, SLAMF1, and FGF-5 between LLV and maintained virological response groups (13). These observations suggest that residual viral activity may be linked to an immune and inflammatory context relevant to antitumor responses. In our exploratory pathway analysis, SIRI showed a statistically significant indirect effect, with an estimated mediated proportion of 9.6%, providing additional support for a possible role of systemic inflammation. Consistent with this immune context, patients with baseline LLV had a lower peripheral CD4/CD8 ratio than those with HBV DNA <20 IU/mL, whereas absolute CD4+ and CD8+ T cell counts were similar between the groups. The CD4/CD8 ratio reflects the balance between helper and cytotoxic T cell compartments and may indicate systemic cellular immune competence. CD4+ T cell help is important for effective cytotoxic CD8+ T cell responses, whereas persistent antigen stimulation can promote CD8+ T cell dysfunction and exhaustion (27, 28). Therefore, the lower CD4/CD8 ratio in patients with LLV may reflect an immune imbalance driven by persistent viral activity, which may weaken antitumor immune surveillance, sustain chronic inflammation, and facilitate immune escape. Similar clinical observations have linked peripheral CD4/CD8 imbalance with treatment response or disease progression in other malignancies, including advanced lung cancer and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (29, 30).The relative importance of viral activity, hepatic reserve, and host immune regulation may vary according to tumor burden and tumor biological activity. This may help explain the subgroup patterns observed in our study. The association was more evident among patients with BCLC stage 0–B disease and AFP ≤400 ng/mL, but less apparent among those with advanced-stage disease or high AFP levels. This pattern may reflect differences in dominant prognostic drivers across disease stages. In patients with lower tumor burden, viral activity and hepatic reserve may remain important contributors to long-term outcomes; in advanced or biologically aggressive disease, tumor progression may dominate prognosis and attenuate the relative contribution of baseline viral status.Beyond establishing the overall prognostic relevance of baseline LLV, further stratification within this subgroup is clinically important. Prediction model development was motivated by the need to refine individualized risk assessment among patients with baseline LLV. The goal was not only to compare survival between baseline virological groups, but also to characterize prognostic heterogeneity within the baseline LLV population. Two complementary models were therefore developed. Model 1 incorporated tumor-related and laboratory variables and was intended for use when complete clinical and imaging information is available. Model 2 was designed as a simplified non-imaging alternative for settings in which detailed imaging-derived tumor variables are incomplete or difficult to standardize. Thus, Model 1 prioritizes predictive performance, whereas Model 2 emphasizes broader applicability in routine clinical practice.The retained predictors captured two major prognostic dimensions: tumor-related burden and aggressiveness, as well as hepatic functional reserve and hepatobiliary injury. In Model 1, tumor size, tumor multiplicity, and PVTT reflected structural tumor burden and vascular invasion (31, 32). AFP, retained in both models, represented tumor biological activity beyond anatomic tumor characteristics (33). CHE, ALP, and GGT reflected hepatic synthetic capacity, cholestasis, and hepatobiliary injury (34–36). Together, these variables suggest that survival among patients with baseline LLV is shaped by both tumor-related factors and the underlying hepatic condition.Consistent with the rationale for dedicated risk stratification, the final RSF implementations of Model 1 and Model 2 showed numerically higher AUCs and generally lower Brier scores than conventional prognostic systems, including Child–Pugh class, BCLC stage, ALBI grade, TNM stage, and MELD score. This finding does not diminish the clinical value of conventional prognostic systems, which remain essential for treatment allocation and broad risk stratification. Instead, the proposed models may provide complementary individualized estimates within the specific subgroup of patients with baseline LLV. To further assess applicability, exploratory analyses across initial HCC treatment groups showed broadly consistent model performance.Beyond model-based risk prediction, the present study suggests that baseline LLV may serve as a practical marker for identifying patients with HBV-HCC who remain at increased risk. Because patients with baseline LLV had poorer survival, this virological phenotype may prompt closer longitudinal monitoring of HBV DNA and liver function during antitumor therapy, together with reassessment of factors that may contribute to incomplete viral suppression, including adherence, antiviral potency, treatment interruption, and possible virological breakthrou…
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a major etiological driver, particularly in regions with a high HBV burden (1, 2). The widespread use of nucleos(t)ide analogs has substantially suppressed HBV replication and reduced the risk of cirrhosis and HCC (3, 4). However, antiviral therapy does not eliminate the risk of liver disease progression or HCC development (5, 6). During nucleos(t)ide analog therapy, patients may achieve maintained virological response, commonly characterized by persistently undetectable HBV DNA or HBV DNA <20 IU/mL, whereas others continue to have persistent or intermittent low-level viremia (LLV), usually defined as HBV DNA levels between 20 and 2000 IU/mL (7, 8). Although LLV has traditionally been regarded as a state of relatively controlled viral replication, increasing evidence suggests that it may not represent a benign virological condition.In chronic HBV infection, LLV has been associated with adverse long-term outcomes. Compared with patients with maintained virological response or undetectable HBV DNA, those with LLV or low but detectable HBV DNA remain at increased risk of HCC development (9–11). Emerging evidence further suggests that low-level HBV replication may retain clinical relevance in patients with established HCC. These findings suggest that residual low-level viral replication may remain prognostically relevant after HCC diagnosis, raising the question of whether baseline LLV may identify a subgroup of patients with HBV-HCC who remain at increased residual risk.Although longitudinal HBV DNA trajectories may provide additional prognostic information during follow-up, baseline HBV DNA is a routinely available measure at the time of initial HCC evaluation. This early virological marker may help identify residual viral activity before subsequent treatment response and follow-up HBV DNA data become available. However, whether baseline LLV is associated with worse survival than baseline HBV DNA <20 IU/mL in a broader HBV-HCC population remains insufficiently clarified. In particular, its prognostic value requires further evaluation across different initial HCC treatment strategies.The biological mechanisms linking LLV to outcomes in HBV-HCC remain incompletely understood. Persistent viral antigen exposure may contribute to impaired HBV-specific T cell responses and immune phenotypes associated with T cell exhaustion, although these alterations appear to be heterogeneous (7, 16). Emerging evidence also suggests that residual viral activity may be linked to host immune dysregulation and response to immunotherapy (13). full_text: Abstract The current study presents a hybrid framework combining deep learning and ensemble learning models to predict hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) based on sequence variants of the hepatitis B virus (HBV)-X gene. In contrast to traditional single-model approaches, the proposed framework integrates deep learning architectures with data balancing and ensemble learning strategies to enhance predictive robustness and generalization. The dataset comprises 3,360 distinct DNA sequences categorized into HCC and Non-HCC classes, with a significant class imbalance favoring the Non-HCC group. To address this issue, the Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to reduce classification bias and improve minority class learning. Two sequence encoding strategies, One-Hot encoding and K-mer encoding (K = 3 and K = 6), were employed to capture nucleotide composition and sequence dependencies. A range of machine learning models, including Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Nu-Support Vector Classifier (NuSVC), Logistic Regression (LR), XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), and AdaBoost, as well as deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), were systematically evaluated. To further enhance predictive performance, a hybrid stacking ensemble framework was developed, integrating a CNN–BiLSTM architecture and Random Forest as base learners, with Logistic Regression serving as the meta-classifier to combine their predictions. All methodological steps, model configurations, and evaluation strategies were explicitly defined to ensure reproducibility and facilitate verification. The proposed hybrid stacking ensemble model demonstrated superior performance compared to individual machine learning and deep learning models. One-Hot encoding consistently outperformed K-mer encoding across most models. The best-performing hybrid stacking ensemble achieved an accuracy of 0.9139 and an F1-score of 0.9126, indicating a strong balance between classification performance and generalization. The application of SMOTE further improved model stability and reduced classification bias. These results highlight that the integration of hybrid deep learning models with ensemble learning and class imbalance correction provides a significant improvement over conventional single-model approaches for HBV-related HCC prediction. The proposed framework has potential applications in clinical diagnostic systems for early and accurate detection of HCC. Future work will focus on external validation using independent datasets and further optimization of encoding strategies and advanced deep learning architectures. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a predictive framework for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) using sequence variants of the hepatitis B virus (HBV)-X gene, addressing the need for improved diagnostic tools in HBV-related HCC detection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a dataset of 3,360 distinct DNA sequences categorized into HCC and Non-HCC classes, with a significant class imbalance favoring the Non-HCC group. The framework was designed to enhance predictive robustness and generalization through integration of deep learning and ensemble learning strategies.
analysis.methods: The study evaluated a range of machine learning models, including Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Nu-Support Vector Classifier (NuSVC), Logistic Regression (LR), XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), and AdaBoost, alongside deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM). A hybrid stacking ensemble framework was developed, integrating a CNN–BiLSTM architecture and Random Forest as base learners, with Logistic Regression serving as the meta-classifier to combine their predictions. The dataset was processed using One-Hot encoding and K-mer encoding (K = 3 and K = 6) to capture nucleotide composition and sequence dependencies.
analysis.main_results: The hybrid stacking ensemble model demonstrated superior performance compared to individual machine learning and deep learning models. One-Hot encoding consistently outperformed K-mer encoding across most models. The best-performing hybrid stacking ensemble achieved an accuracy of 0.9139 and an F1-score of 0.9126, indicating a strong balance between classification performance and generalization.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating that the integration of hybrid deep learning models with ensemble learning and class imbalance correction significantly improves HCC prediction from HBV-X gene sequence variants compared to conventional single-model approaches.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the proposed framework could be applied in clinical diagnostic systems for early and accurate detection of HBV-related hepatocellular carcinoma, potentially enhancing public health outcomes through improved screening and intervention strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results are based on a single dataset and require external validation using independent datasets to confirm generalizability. The evidence is strong, as all methodological steps, model configurations, and evaluation strategies were explicitly defined.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a hybrid framework combining deep learning and ensemble learning models to predict hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) from sequence variants of the hepatitis B virus (HBV)-X gene. The dataset included 3,360 DNA sequences with a significant class imbalance, which was addressed using SMOTE. Two encoding strategies, One-Hot and K-mer, were tested, with One-Hot showing better performance. A hybrid stacking ensemble model, integrating CNN–BiLSTM and Random Forest with Logistic Regression as the meta-classifier, achieved high accuracy (0.9139) and F1-score (0.9126). The authors interpret these results as a significant improvement over conventional single-model approaches for HBV-related HCC prediction. The framework has potential applications in clinical diagnostics for early detection of HCC. However, the study requires external validation to confirm its generalizability. The evidence is strong due to the explicit definition of all methodological steps and evaluation strategies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在利用 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV)-X 基因的序列变异开发肝细胞癌 (HCC) 的预测框架,以满足改进 HBV 相关 HCC 检测诊断工具的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 3,360 个不同 DNA 序列的数据集,分为 HCC 和非 HCC 类别,其中明显的类别不平衡有利于非 HCC 组。该框架旨在通过深度学习和集成学习策略的集成来增强预测的鲁棒性和泛化性。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究评估了一系列机器学习模型,包括多项式朴素贝叶斯 (MNB)、支持 媒介 分类器 (SVC)、Nu-Support 媒介 分类器 (NuSVC)、逻辑回归 (LR)、XGBoost、随机森林 (RF) 和 AdaBoost,以及卷积神经网络 (CNN) 和双向长短期记忆 (BiLSTM) 等深度学习模型。开发了一个混合堆叠集成框架,集成了 CNN-BiLSTM 架构和随机森林作为基础学习器,逻辑回归作为元分类器来组合它们的预测。使用 One-Hot 编码和 K-mer 编码(K = 3 和 K = 6)处理数据集,以捕获核苷酸组成和序列依赖性。
elements_zh.main_results: 与单独的机器学习和深度学习模型相比,混合堆叠集成模型表现出了卓越的性能。在大多数模型中,One-Hot 编码的性能始终优于 K-mer 编码。表现最好的混合堆叠集成实现了 0.9139 的准确率和 0.9126 的 F1 分数,表明分类性能和泛化之间的强大平衡。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将结果解释为,与传统的单一模型方法相比,混合深度学习模型与集成学习和类别不平衡校​​正的集成显着改善了 HBV-X 基因序列变异的 HCC 预测。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,所提出的框架可以应用于临床诊断系统,以早期、准确地检测乙型肝炎病毒相关的肝细胞癌,从而通过改进筛查和干预策略来潜在地改善公共卫生结果。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于单个数据集,需要使用独立数据集进行外部验证以确认普遍性。证据是强有力的,因为所有方法步骤、模型配置和评估策略都被明确定义。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在利用 乙型肝炎病毒 (HBV)-X 基因的序列变异开发肝细胞癌 (HCC) 的预测框架,以满足改进 HBV 相关 HCC 检测诊断工具的需求。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 3,360 个不同 DNA 序列的数据集,分为 HCC 和非 HCC 类别,其中明显的类别不平衡有利于非 HCC 组。该框架旨在通过深度学习和集成学习策略的集成来增强预测的鲁棒性和泛化性。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究评估了一系列机器学习模型,包括多项式朴素贝叶斯 (MNB)、支持 媒介 分类器 (SVC)、Nu-Support 媒介 分类器 (NuSVC)、逻辑回归 (LR)、XGBoost、随机森林 (RF) 和 AdaBoost,以及卷积神经网络 (CNN) 和双向长短期记忆 (BiLSTM) 等深度学习模型。开发了一个混合堆叠集成框架,集成了 CNN-BiLSTM 架构和随机森林作为基础学习器,逻辑回归作为元分类器来组合它们的预测。使用 One-Hot 编码和 K-mer 编码(K = 3 和 K = 6)处理数据集,以捕获核苷酸组成和序列依赖性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 与单独的机器学习和深度学习模型相比,混合堆叠集成模型表现出了卓越的性能。在大多数模型中,One-Hot 编码的性能始终优于 K-mer 编码。表现最好的混合堆叠集成实现了 0.9139 的准确率和 0.9126 的 F1 分数,表明分类性能和泛化之间的强大平衡。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将结果解释为,与传统的单一模型方法相比,混合深度学习模型与集成学习和类别不平衡校​​正的集成显着改善了 HBV-X 基因序列变异的 HCC 预测。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,所提出的框架可以应用于临床诊断系统,以早期、准确地检测乙型肝炎病毒相关的肝细胞癌,从而通过改进筛查和干预策略来潜在地改善公共卫生结果。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于单个数据集,需要使用独立数据集进行外部验证以确认普遍性。证据是强有力的,因为所有方法步骤、模型配置和评估策略都被明确定义。

Hepatitis B update: enabling progress towards elimination. Aust Prescr 2026;49:160-7.https://doi.org/10.18773/austprescr.2026.043 Hepatitis B is a common vaccine-preventable and treatable condition. Chronic hepatitis B is often asymptomatic and can be missed if the diagnosis is not actively considered. The World Health Organization and the Australian Government have committed to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat by 2030. The tools required to achieve this are available: an effective vaccine, accurate blood tests for diagnosis and monitoring, effective antiviral treatments and access to ultrasound to enable early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. Risk-based testing approaches are not effective enough to enable Australia to achieve elimination targets; hence, the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025â2030 calls for population-wide testing to identify hepatitis B status. Chronic hepatitis B is a lifelong disease that requires long-term monitoring and follow-up irrespective of the stage of disease or whether an individual is taking antiviral treatment. Most healthcare for people living with chronic hepatitis B can be provided in primary care. All medical practitioners and authorised nurse practitioners can now prescribe antiviral therapy for hepatitis B; additional accreditation is no longer required. Holistic care includes the provision of resources in a personâs preferred language, peer and cultural support workers, access to a long-term effective model of care, and appropriate monitoring. Continuity of healthcare providers is desirable and an important enabler of sustained engagement in care. One-third of the worldâs population has been exposed to hepatitis B, with an estimated 254 million people currently living with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).1 An estimated 227,000 people are living with CHB in Australia.2 The hepatitis B virus is the second most potent carcinogen after tobacco,3 increasing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by its very presence. Therefore, unlike other causes of hepatitis, such as hepatitis C, where significant liver fibrosis or cirrhosis needs to be present before HCC risk increases, people living with CHB have an increased risk of HCC irrespective of their cirrhotic status. CHB causes inflammation of the liver that can progress to cirrhosis and HCC. One-quarter of people with untreated CHB will die from either HCC or liver failure.4 Although treatment does not cure the infection, it can prevent progression to cirrhosis and reduces the risk of HCC. In 2016, the World Health Assembly committed to the elimination of hepatitis B as a major public health threat by 2030, and an elimination strategy was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO).5 Australiaâs ongoing commitment to this elimination goal is reiterated in the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025â2030.6 Despite having all the necessary tools to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat, it is estimated that in Australia, 1 in 3 of the 227,000 people living with CHB are not aware of their diagnosis and only 1 in 4 are receiving guideline-based care. In addition, only small increases in the uptake of antiviral treatment have been seen over the past decade.2 Many barriers to accessing testing, diagnosis and care exist, including (but not limited to) the asymptomatic nature of CHB, a lack of knowledge and understanding of risk factors, stigma, remoteness, the logistics of accessing care through tertiary services, English commonly not being a patientâs first language and systematic consequences of a CHB diagnosis, particularly in the immigration system. Elimination requires a paradigm shift in the care provided to people living with CHB to increase: - hepatitis B testing through population-wide universal offer of testing, treatment, enabling earlier diagnosis - primary care provision of hepatitis B testing, follow-up and long-term monitoring of those living with CHB - the number of people on treatment. Any changes in the approach to hepatitis B management need to be developed in consultation with affected individuals and communities to ensure stigma and discrimination are addressed and to minimise the personal and social impacts of hepatitis B.7 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia are disproportionately impacted by CHB, with an overall prevalence of 3.4%, compared with 0.8% for Australia as a whole, increasing to more than 6% in some regions.8 Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory have a unique subgenotype of hepatitis B virus (HBV/C4) that has genotypic and phenotypic markers of faster progression to cirrhosis and increased risk of HCC, which further increases the urgency for early diagnosis and engagement in care. Some people born overseas are also at higher risk of CHB for many different reasons, predominantly influenced by the prevalence of CHB in the country they were born in and the availability of a hepatitis vaccine as part of the infant vaccine schedule in that country. This article aims to provide an update and guidance for healthcare professionals across Australia to play their part in the elimination of CHB. People living with CHB are often asymptomatic and may have normal liver function tests, so an active case-finding approach is needed. A simple and cheap blood test for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) is all that is required to establish hepatitis B immune status, including the need for vaccination, or for the diagnosis of CHB. Further testing is needed to diagnose and distinguish between acute and chronic infection (IgM anti-HBc) and to assess infectivity and inform decisions about treatment (hepatitis B envelope antigen [HBeAg] and hepatitis B virus [HBV] DNA). Historically, the national testing policy had a risk-based approach to diagnosis except for the universal testing recommendation for pregnant women as a part of antenatal care. High-risk groups identified for routine testing included (but were not limited to) Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, healthcare workers and people born in high CHB-prevalence countries. However, this approach is not effective enough to meet the goal of eliminating hepatitis B by 2030 because, currently in Australia, an estimated 32.6% of people living with CHB are unaware of their diagnosis.2 Hence, the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025â2030 recommends universal testing for all adults as a priority action to ensure all Australians know their hepatitis B status.6 There are clear recommended care pathways for hepatitis B prevention and management for all combinations of hepatitis B antigen and antibody results (Table 1). Table 1 Interpreting and acting on hepatitis B test results9 | Test | Result | Interpretation | Hepatitis B status | Action | | HbsAg | Negative | Susceptible | Nonimmune | Add hepatitis B status to patient medical summary Offer hepatitis B vaccination If the person requires proof of immunity (i.e. household or sexual contact), repeat serology 4 to 8 weeks after primary course or booster to determine whether anti-HBs is positive. If it is not, give a booster dose and recheck serology 4 to 8 weeks later | | Anti-HBc | Negative | | | | | Anti-HBs | Negative [NB1] | | | | | HBsAg | Negative | Resolved hepatitis B infection | Immune by exposure | Add hepatitis B status to patient medical summary No further action â do not test again If patient becomes immunocompromised or develops unexplained abnormal liver function tests, reassess and retest | | Anti-HBc | Positive | | | | | Anti-HBs | Positive [NB2] | | | | | HBsAg | Negative | Vaccinated | Immune by vaccination | Add hepatitis B status to patient medical summary No further action â do not test again Hepatitis B vaccine booster doses are recommended in immunosuppressed individuals, including those with renal failure or HIV infection | | Anti-HBc | Negative | | | | | Anti-HBs | Positive [NB2] | | | | | HBsAg | Positive | Acute infection This serology pattern can also be seen in people who are living with CHB and are experiencing a flare of hepatitis | Acute infection | Add hepatitis B status to patient medical summary Order further tests as per âClinical careâ row in Table 2 Perform contact tracing Provide counselling and support Repeat serology in 6 months to see whether HBsAg is negative | | Anti-HBc | Positive | | | | | Anti-HBs | Negative [NB1] | | | | | IgM anti-HBc | Positive | | | | | HBsAg | Positive | Chronic infection | Chronic infection | Add hepatitis B status to patient medical summary Develop CHB care plan with 6-monthly recalls in patient record for ongoing testing, monitoring and follow-up Initiate antiviral treatment in eligible patients (Table 3) Perform contact tracing Provide counselling and support Ensure that the person has had their diagnosis and care requirements explained in their preferred language | | Anti-HBc | Positive | | | | | Anti-HBs | Negative [NB1] | | | | | IgM anti-HBc | Negative | | | | | anti-HBc = hepatitis B core antibody; Testing should be considered for everyone who does not have their hepatitis B status documented, irrespective of their vaccination history. Historically, treatment of CHB has been provided in tertiary care settings or by general practitioners (GPs) and nurse practitioners (NPs) with additional prescribing training through the section 100 (s100) access scheme. After years of advocacy to increase the number of prescribers and improve access to treatment, specialist accreditation requirements for prescribing hepatitis B antiviral drugs in Australia were removed on 1 September 2026.11 All medical practitioners and authorised nurse practitioners can now prescribe subsidised hepatitis B antiviral treatments for eligible patients under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, addressing a longstanding barrier to the delivery of CHB care. Prescriber education and support continue to be available through ASHM (the Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine), including the Hepatitis B Advanced Management and Prescribing Course (formerly the s100 prescriber accreditation course). Despite the availability of effective antiviral treatments, only around 13% of people with CHB are on antiviral treatment, representing approximately one-third of those who would benefit from treatment according to current Australian guidelines.2 Newer international guidelines have expanded treatment recommendations to include a much broader group of those living with CHB.1,12 Where care has been decentralised and provided predominantly in primary care, the number of people on treatment has increased significantly. For example, a highly collaborative program developed in the Northern Territory, the Hep B PAST program, achieved engagement in CHB care for 86% of people with CHB, with 24% on treatment,13 using the same definitions as the national hepatitis B mapping project.2 The main principles of the Hep B PAST model are as follows: - Systematically identify everyone in a practice who is living with CHB by testing and documenting hepatitis B status in the health record of all patients. - Offer vaccination to those people who are not immune. - Enable holistic care to be provided to those people who are living with CHB as per current Australian guidelines. The Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025â2030 recommends models of care, such as Hep B PAST, be rolled out to other parts of Australia. Once a diagnosis of CHB has been established, a holistic baseline assessment and a plan for ongoing care are needed. Assessment may require several consultations and, in some patients, may require the use of interpreters and peer workers, where available. This assessment can be split into 4 main sections (Table 2): - Patient understanding â education and explanation of hepatitis B diagnosis in the patientâs preferred language - Clinical care â assessment and associated investigations to identify the extent of liver damage and comorbidities, identify those who are eligible for antiviral treatment and formulate a comprehensive care plan - Contact tracing â consideration of who else needs to be tested within the patientâs family and close networks - Social and cultural needs â active consideration of cultural, social and legal needs, and stigma, as appropriate Table 2 Assessment of people diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B | Care domain | What is required | How can it be provided | | 1. Elimination requires a paradigm shift in the care provided to people living with CHB to increase: - hepatitis B testing through population-wide universal offer of testing, treatment, enabling earlier diagnosis - primary care provision of hepatitis B testing, follow-up and long-term monitoring of those living with CHB - the number of people on treatment. Any changes in the approach to hepatitis B management need to be developed in consultation with affected individuals and communities to ensure stigma and discrimination are addressed and to minimise the personal and social impacts of hepatitis B.7 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia are disproportionately impacted by CHB, with an overall prevalence of 3.4%, compared with 0.8% for Australia as a whole, increasing to more than 6% in some regions.8 Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory have a unique subgenotype of hepatitis B virus (HBV/C4) that has genotypic and phenotypic markers of faster progression to cirrhosis and increased risk of HCC, which further increases the urgency for early diagnosis and engagement in care. Some people born overseas are also at higher risk of CHB for many different reasons, predominantly influenced by the prevalence of CHB in the country they were born in and the availability of a hepatitis vaccine as part of the infant vaccine schedule in that country. This article aims to provide an update and guidance for healthcare professionals across Australia to play their part in the elimination of CHB. People living with CHB are often asymptomatic and may have normal liver function tests, so an active case-finding approach is needed. A simple and cheap blood test for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) is all that is required to establish hepatitis B immune status, including the need for vaccination, or for the diagnosis of CHB. Further testing is needed to diagnose and distinguish between acute and chronic infection (IgM anti-HBc) and to assess infectivity and inform decisions about treatment (hepatitis B envelope antigen [HBeAg] and hepatitis B virus [HBV] DNA). Historically, the national testing policy had a risk-based approach to diagnosis except for the universal testing recommendation for pregnant women as a part of antenatal care. High-risk groups identified for routine testing included (but were not limited to) Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, healthcare workers and people born in high CHB-prevalence countries. However, this approach is not effective enough to meet the goal of eliminating hepatitis B by 2030 because, currently in Australia, an estimated 32.6% of people living with CHB are unaware of their diagnosis.2 Hence, the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025â2030 recommends universal testing for all adults as a priority action to ensure all Australians know their hepatitis B status.6 There are clear recommended care pathways for hepatitis B prevention and management for all combinations of hepatitis B antigen and antibody results (Table 1). title_original: Hepatitis B update: enabling progress towards elimination

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for improved hepatitis B management and elimination strategies, highlighting the challenges in diagnosing and treating chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in Australia.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review of hepatitis B management practices in Australia, focusing on high-risk groups such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, healthcare workers, and individuals born in high CHB-prevalence countries. It reports that 32.6% of people living with CHB are unaware of their diagnosis.
analysis.methods: The study uses a combination of national data, policy analysis, and program evaluations to assess current practices and barriers in hepatitis B testing, diagnosis, and treatment. It references the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025–2030 and the Hep B PAST program as examples of interventions.
analysis.main_results: The study found that only 13% of people with CHB are on antiviral treatment, despite the availability of effective therapies. It also highlights that Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory have a unique subgenotype (HBV/C4) associated with faster progression to cirrhosis and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the current risk-based testing approach is insufficient for eliminating hepatitis B by 2030, and that universal testing for all adults is a necessary step. The novelty lies in the emphasis on community-specific subgenotypes and their implications for treatment urgency.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for universal testing and improved access to treatment for CHB, particularly in high-risk populations. They also highlight the importance of addressing social determinants and cultural factors in hepatitis B care.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on existing national data and policy documents, which may not capture real-world implementation challenges. The evidence is moderate, as it relies on observational data rather than experimental results.

analysis.summary_en: This review highlights the challenges in diagnosing and treating chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in Australia, emphasizing the need for universal testing to meet elimination goals by 2030. It reports that 32.6% of people with CHB are unaware of their diagnosis, and that Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory have a unique subgenotype (HBV/C4) linked to faster progression to cirrhosis and increased HCC risk. The study advocates for a holistic approach to care, including patient education and community engagement, and notes that the removal of specialist accreditation requirements for prescribing antiviral drugs has improved access to treatment. While the evidence is moderate, the findings underscore the importance of addressing social and cultural barriers to effective hepatitis B management.

full_text: Dear Editor, The triple elimination initiative is a global effort to stop the transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B from mother to child and aligns with Sustainable Development Goal—3. The initiative’s focus include: care for exposed infants by following up with infants who are exposed to HIV, syphilis, or hepatitis B; infant feeding thus ensuring infants are fed optimally; treatment for mothers by providing lifelong treatment and care for mothers who are living with HIV and capacity expansion through increasing the capacity of maternal and child health services to address the vertical transmission of other communicable diseases.[] West Bengal has been the first state in India to take the call on Triple Elimination of Vertical Transmission of HIV Syphilis and Hepatitis B in July ’23. The state government of West Bengal, India, in partnership with WHO and William J Clinton Foundation, conducted a demonstration pilot of targeted triple elimination interventions. A State Task Force was formally constituted to steer the course along with a Technical Advisory Group. A situational assessment was carried out across four districts as a prelude (September to October 2023). The project started right from antenatal check-up by women, followed by medical intervention to prevent vertical transmission. While Bengal is already doing better than the national average of 40% for hepatitis B, 96% against 84% for HIV and 64% against 57% for syphilis, health officials said scaling up testing and intervention was aimed at intensifying its efforts. This was followed by a series of consultations which culminated in the Kolkata Commitment of December 2023 with a call to Elimination of HIV Syphilis and Hepatitis B by 2026.[] Efforts focused on increasing the uptake of screening, improving data-sharing mechanisms for linkages, and training facility staff in integrated service flows. Initial results from the pilot found that these methods enhanced case finding and improved testing and treatment coverage of exposed infants. Further scale-up is planned across the entire state. Necessary Governance Framework, Standard Operating Procedures and Tools based on Situational Assessment findings were put in place. The pilot covered a population of 56,44,075 with 2,33,605 annual estimated pregnancies across the four districts. The focus has been on an integrated effort at universal screening of pregnant women, early linkage to care and retention across the care cascade. The integrated effort involves the Maternal and Child Health, Routine Immunization, HIV / STI and the Viral Hepatitis services. The state is now scaling up to all 28 districts from January 2025, building on the experience and evidence garnered from the pilot in four districts. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts of interest. REFERENCES - 1. World Health Organization. Regional Office for the Western Pacific (2018). full_text: Abstract Background Hepatitis B is not only one of the most severe infectious diseases in the world, but also an important public health issue facing China. This study aims to build an optimal prediction model for the incidence rate of hepatitis B in China and provide accurate prediction for early monitoring and early warning of infectious diseases. Methods We systematically analyzed the incidence trend of hepatitis B in China based on the monthly incidence data from January 2001 to February 2026. We established a series of time series and machine learning models. On this basis, we tried to predict the incidence of hepatitis B in the medium and long term by fitting the optimal discriminant model of LSTM + CNN. Results The prevalence and incidence rate of hepatitis B in the world and China are decreasing year by year, and China is higher than the global average as well as the mortality rate among elderly people aged 55 and above in China is lower than the global average. The average monthly incidence rate of hepatitis B in China was approximately 0.7 per 10,000 from January 2001 to February 2026. All time series models can capture the trend of incidence rate of hepatitis B. The prediction performance of LSTM + CNN hybrid models (R2 = 0.603) is superior to traditional time series models (exponential smoothing ARIMA and SVR) and individual machine learning models (CNN, GRU, and LSTM). Conclusions LSTM + CNN model demonstrates competitive performance to predict the monthly average incidence rate of hepatitis B in China. The hybrid deep learning model (LSTM + CNN) has shown great potential in time series prediction, although further validation is needed. This study explores effective methods for predicting infectious disease time series models, providing a new perspective for infectious disease prediction studies. title: Semi-quantitative ultrasound scoring reveals hepatic structural recovery and immune modulation during tenofovir alafenamide therapy in chronic hepatitis B
abstract: Objective This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic response to tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using a semi-quantitative ultrasound (US) scoring system, and to investigate the correlation between sonographic changes and immune function restoration. Methods A total of 100 CHB patients who received TAF monotherapy (25 mg/day) for at least 24 months were retrospectively enrolled. A seven-parameter semi-quantitative US score, encompassing liver echogenicity, capsular contour, margin shape, vessel clarity, portal vein diameter (PVD), spleen thickness (ST), and splenic vein velocity (SVV), was calculated at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months. Concurrently, serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), peripheral T-cell subsets, including cluster of differentiation 3-positive (CD3 + ), CD4 + , CD8 + T cells, CD4+/CD8+ ratio, and natural killer (NK) cell activity were measured. Correlations between US scores and biochemical/immune parameters were analyzed. Results At 24 months, all patients achieved HBV DNA <20 IU/mL, with ALT and AST normalization rates of 92% and 95%, respectively. The comprehensive US score decreased significantly from 7.86 ± 1.73 at baseline to 3.37 ± 0.95 at 24 months ( P < 0.001), with the most pronounced improvements observed in capsular smoothness and parenchymal homogeneity. The CD4 + T-cell proportion and CD4 + /CD8 + ratio increased, whereas the CD8 + proportion decreased; NK cell activity rose from 42.7 ± 7.3% to 52.4 ± 6.2% ( P < 0.05). The US score was positively correlated with ALT (r = 0.56) and AST (r = 0.47), and negatively correlated with the CD4 + /CD8 + ratio (r = −0.46) and NK cell activity (r = −0.38) (all P < 0.01). Conclusion These findings indicate that TAF not only suppresses viral replication and normalises liver enzymes but also promotes measurable structural liver improvement, as reflected by declining semi-quantitative US scores. The strong correlations of US scores with biochemical and immune parameters support its utility as a non-invasive imaging biomarker for monitoring treatment efficacy and hepatic repair.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the therapeutic response to tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using a semi-quantitative ultrasound (US) scoring system. It aimed to assess the correlation between sonographic changes and immune function restoration. A total of 100 CHB patients on TAF monotherapy for at least 24 months were enrolled. The US score, which included seven parameters, was calculated at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months. Serum HBV DNA, ALT, AST, and immune parameters were also measured. title_zh: 半定量超声评分揭示慢性乙型肝炎(慢性乙型肝炎)在接受替诺福韦艾拉酚胺治疗期间肝脏结构恢复和免疫调节
source_body_en: Objective This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic response to tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using a semi-quantitative ultrasound (US) scoring system, and to investigate the correlation between sonographic changes and immune function restoration. Methods A total of 100 CHB patients who received TAF monotherapy (25 mg/day) for at least 24 months were retrospectively enrolled. A seven-parameter semi-quantitative US score, encompassing liver echogenicity, capsular contour, margin shape, vessel clarity, portal vein diameter (PVD), spleen thickness (ST), and splenic vein velocity (SVV), was calculated at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months. Concurrently, serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), peripheral T-cell subsets, including cluster of differentiation 3-positive (CD3 + ), CD4 + , CD8 + T cells, CD4+/CD8+ ratio, and natural killer (NK) cell activity were measured. Correlations between US scores and biochemical/immune parameters were analyzed. Results At 24 months, all patients achieved HBV DNA <20 IU/mL, with ALT and AST normalization rates of 92% and 95%, respectively. The comprehensive US score decreased significantly from 7.86 ± 1.73 at baseline to 3.37 ± 0.95 at 24 months ( P < 0.001), with the most pronounced improvements observed in capsular smoothness and parenchymal homogeneity. The CD4 + T-cell proportion and CD4 + /CD8 + ratio increased, whereas the CD8 + proportion decreased; NK cell activity rose from 42.7 ± 7.3% to 52.4 ± 6.2% ( P < 0.05). The US score was positively correlated with ALT (r = 0.56) and AST (r = 0.47), and negatively correlated with the CD4 + /CD8 + ratio (r = −0.46) and NK cell activity (r = −0.38) (all P < 0.01). Conclusion These findings indicate that TAF not only suppresses viral replication and normalises liver enzymes but also promotes measurable structural liver improvement, as reflected by declining semi-quantitative US scores. The strong correlations of US scores with biochemical and immune parameters support its utility as a non-invasive imaging biomarker for monitoring treatment efficacy and hepatic repair.
abstract_zh: 本研究旨在利用半定量超声(US)评分系统评估替诺福韦艾拉酚胺二甲基磺酸盐(TAF)在慢性乙型肝炎(慢性乙型肝炎)患者中的治疗反应,并探讨超声影像变化与免疫功能恢复之间的相关性。方法 入选了100例接受TAF单药治疗(25 mg/天)至少24个月的慢性乙型肝炎患者进行回顾性分析。在基线、12个月和24个月时计算了包含肝脏回声、包膜轮廓、边缘形态、血管清晰度、门静脉直径(PVD)、脾脏厚度(ST)和脾静脉血流速度(SVV)的七参数半定量超声评分。同时测量了血清乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)脱氧核糖核酸(DNA)、丙氨酸氨基转移酶(ALT)、天门冬氨酸氨基转移酶(AST)以及外周T细胞亚群,包括分化簇3阳性(CD3+)、CD4+、CD8+ T细胞、CD4+/CD8+比值和自然杀伤(NK)细胞活性。分析了超声评分与生化和免疫参数之间的相关性。结果 在24个月时,所有患者均达到HBV DNA <20 IU/mL,ALT和AST的正常化率分别为92%和95%。综合超声评分从基线的7.86 ± 1.73显著下降至24个月的3.37 ± 0.95(P < 0.001),其中包膜平滑度和实质均匀性的改善最为显著。CD4+ T细胞比例和CD4+/CD8+比值增加,而CD8+ T细胞比例下降;NK细胞活性从42.7 ± 7.3%上升至52.4 ± 6.2%(P < 0.05)。超声评分与ALT(r = 0.56)和AST(r = 0.47)呈正相关,与CD4+/CD8+比值(r = −0.46)和NK细胞活性(r = −0.38)呈负相关(所有P < 0.01)。结论 这些发现表明,TAF不仅抑制病毒复制并使肝酶正常化,还促进可测量的肝脏结构改善,这体现在半定量超声评分的下降。超声评分与生化和免疫参数之间的强相关性支持其作为非侵入性影像生物标志物用于监测治疗疗效和肝脏修复的潜力。
